To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) when a beam is incident near the critical angle on an interface between a dielectric and vacuum it will be deflected from the direction predicted for Snell's law by Fresnel filtering, (b) the effect can be quite substantial, and (c) this effect is of particular importance in dielectric microcavities, which are used in microcavity lasers, and in other applications.

the Fresnel filtering effect causes a deviation from Snell's Law that is important for microcavity lasers, and this effect is due to the fact that the Fresnel coefficients depend on the angle of incidence.

the angular deviation of a beam incident on a dielectric interface at an angle near the critical angle can be quite large and that it is a consequence of the Fresnel filtering that occurs in the evanescent field region.

the physics of optical microcavity lasers in the regime where the optical confinement is provided by the index difference between the cavity material and the surrounding medium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of the Fresnel filter is to reduce the effective gain for a given mode by a factor that is a function of the mode number.
the effect of Fresnel filtering on the far field of a laser is to cause a deflection from the Snell's law angle.
the effect of Fresnel filtering on the emission of microcavity lasers is negligible, except in the special case of a laser with a very small mode volume, where it is important.

we are showing how to design microcavity lasers with very high output powers, and with a very narrow divergence.
